source: To make them run easily and swiftly, the axles of carriages are anointed; and for much the same purpose, some whalers perform an analogous operation upon their boat; they grease the bottom. Nor is it to be doubted that as such a procedure can do no harm, it may possibly be of no contemptible advantage; considering that oil and water are hostile; that oil is a sliding thing, and that the object in view is to make the boat slide bravely. Queequeg believed strongly in anointing his boat, and one morning not long after the German ship Jungfrau disappeared, took more than customary pains in that occupation; crawling under its bottom, where it hung over the side, and rubbing in the unctuousness as though diligently seeking to insure a crop of hair from the craft’s bald keel. He seemed to be working in obedience to some particular presentiment. Nor did it remain unwarranted by the event.
Towards noon whales were raised; but so soon as the ship sailed down to them, they turned and fled with swift precipitancy; a disordered flight, as of Cleopatra’s barges from Actium.

Nevertheless, the boats pursued, and Stubb’s was foremost. By great exertion, Tashtego at last succeeded in planting one iron; but the stricken whale, without at all sounding, still continued his horizontal flight, with added fleetness. Such unintermitted strainings upon the planted iron must sooner or later inevitably extract it. It became imperative to lance the flying whale, or be content to lose him. But to haul the boat up to his flank was impossible, he swam so fast and furious. What then remained?

Of all the wondrous devices and dexterities, the sleights of hand and countless subtleties, to which the veteran whaleman is so often forced, none exceed that fine manœuvre with the lance called pitchpoling. Small sword, or broad sword, in all its exercises boasts nothing like it. It is only indispensable with an inveterate running whale; its grand fact and feature is the wonderful distance to which the long lance is accurately darted from a violently rocking, jerking boat, under extreme headway. Steel and wood included, the entire spear is some ten or twelve feet in length; the staff is much slighter than that of the harpoon, and also of a lighter material—pine. It is furnished with a small rope called a warp, of considerable length, by which it can be hauled back to the hand after darting.

But before going further, it is important to mention here, that though the harpoon may be pitchpoled in the same way with the lance, yet it is seldom done; and when done, is still less frequently successful, on account of the greater weight and inferior length of the harpoon as compared with the lance, which in effect become serious drawbacks. As a general thing, therefore, you must first get fast to a whale, before any pitchpoling comes into play.

Look now at Stubb; a man who from his humorous, deliberate coolness and equanimity in the direst emergencies, was specially qualified to excel in pitchpoling. Look at him; he stands upright in the tossed bow of the flying boat; wrapt in fleecy foam, the towing whale is forty feet ahead. Handling the long lance lightly, glancing twice or thrice along its length to see if it be exactly straight, Stubb whistlingly gathers up the coil of the warp in one hand, so as to secure its free end in his grasp, leaving the rest unobstructed. Then holding the lance full before his waistband’s middle, he levels it at the whale; when, covering him with it, he steadily depresses the butt-end in his hand, thereby elevating the point till the weapon stands fairly balanced upon his palm, fifteen feet in the air. He minds you somewhat of a juggler, balancing a long staff on his chin. Next moment with a rapid, nameless impulse, in a superb lofty arch the bright steel spans the foaming distance, and quivers in the life spot of the whale. Instead of sparkling water, he now spouts red blood.

“That drove the spigot out of him!” cried Stubb. “’Tis July’s immortal Fourth; all fountains must run wine today! Would now, it were old Orleans whiskey, or old Ohio, or unspeakable old Monongahela! Then, Tashtego, lad, I’d have ye hold a canakin to the jet, and we’d drink round it! Yea, verily, hearts alive, we’d brew choice punch in the spread of his spout-hole there, and from that live punch-bowl quaff the living stuff.”

Again and again to such gamesome talk, the dexterous dart is repeated, the spear returning to its master like a greyhound held in skilful leash. The agonized whale goes into his flurry; the tow-line is slackened, and the pitchpoler dropping astern, folds his hands, and mutely watches the monster die.

modern_en.title: Chapter 84 — Pitchpoling
paragraphs: To make them run easily and swiftly, the axles of carriages are anointed; and for much the same purpose, some whalers perform a similar operation on their boats — they grease the bottom. Nor can it be doubted that, since such a procedure can do no harm, it may possibly be of no small advantage, considering that oil and water are hostile, that oil is a sliding thing, and that the object in view is to make the boat slide bravely along. Queequeg believed strongly in anointing his boat, and one morning, not long after the German ship Jungfrau disappeared, he took more than his usual pains over it, crawling under its bottom where it hung over the side and rubbing in the grease as though he were diligently trying to raise a crop of hair on the craft's bald keel. He seemed to be acting on some particular premonition. Nor did what followed prove it unfounded.
Toward noon whales were sighted; but as soon as the ship sailed down on them, they turned and fled in headlong haste — a disordered flight, like that of Cleopatra's barges from Actium.

Nevertheless, the boats gave chase, and Stubb's was in the lead. With great effort, Tashtego at last managed to plant one iron; but the stricken whale, without sounding at all, kept up his horizontal flight, even faster than before. Such unbroken strain on the planted iron must sooner or later inevitably pull it out. It became essential to lance the fleeing whale, or be content to lose him. But hauling the boat up to his flank was impossible; he swam so fast and furiously. What was left, then?

Of all the wondrous devices and skills, the sleights of hand and countless subtleties that the veteran whaleman is so often driven to, none surpass that fine maneuver with the lance called pitchpoling. Neither small sword nor broadsword, in all its drills, can boast anything like it. It is indispensable only with a whale that is a stubborn runner; its great feature and fact is the wonderful distance to which the long lance is accurately thrown from a violently rocking, jerking boat racing ahead at full speed. Steel and wood included, the whole spear is some ten or twelve feet long; the shaft is much slighter than the harpoon's, and of a lighter material too — pine. It is fitted with a small rope of considerable length, called a warp, by which it can be hauled back to the hand after the throw.

But before going further, it is important to mention here that although the harpoon may be pitchpoled in the same way as the lance, it is seldom done; and when it is, it succeeds still less often, because of the harpoon's greater weight and shorter length compared with the lance, which in practice become serious drawbacks. As a general rule, therefore, you must first get fast to a whale before any pitchpoling comes into play.

Look now at Stubb — a man whose humorous, deliberate coolness and composure in the direst emergencies made him especially fit to excel at pitchpoling. Look at him: he stands upright in the tossing bow of the flying boat; wrapped in fleecy foam, the towing whale is forty feet ahead. Handling the long lance lightly, glancing two or three times along its length to see that it is exactly straight, Stubb, whistling, gathers up the coil of the warp in one hand, so as to keep its free end in his grip and leave the rest unobstructed. Then, holding the lance squarely in front of the middle of his waistband, he levels it at the whale; and, keeping it trained on him, he steadily presses down the butt-end in his hand, thereby raising the point until the weapon stands neatly balanced on his palm, fifteen feet in the air. He reminds you a little of a juggler balancing a long staff on his chin. The next moment, with a rapid, nameless impulse, the bright steel spans the foaming distance in a superb, lofty arc and quivers in the whale's life-spot. Instead of sparkling water, he now spouts red blood.

"That drove the spigot out of him!" cried Stubb. "It's the immortal Fourth of July; all fountains must run wine today! If only it were old Orleans whiskey, or old Ohio, or unspeakable old Monongahela! Then, Tashtego, lad, I'd have you hold a mug to the jet, and we'd drink a round from it! Yes, truly, my hearties, we'd brew choice punch in the spread of his spout-hole there, and from that live punch-bowl drink down the living stuff."

Again and again, to such playful talk, the deft throw is repeated, the spear returning to its master like a greyhound held on a skillful leash. The agonized whale goes into his flurry, the convulsion of his death; the towline is slackened, and the pitchpoler, dropping astern, folds his hands and silently watches the monster die.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 84 — Pitchpoling
paragraphs: For at få dem til at løbe let og hurtigt smører man akslerne på vogne; og til omtrent samme formål foretager nogle hvalfangere en lignende behandling af deres både — de smører bunden. Og man kan ikke tvivle på, at når en sådan fremgangsmåde ikke kan gøre skade, kan den muligvis være til ikke ringe gavn, i betragtning af at olie og vand er fjender, at olie er noget glidende, og at hensigten er at få båden til at glide tappert af sted. Queequeg troede stærkt på at smøre sin båd, og en morgen, ikke længe efter at det tyske skib Jungfrau forsvandt, gjorde han sig større umage end sædvanligt, krøb ind under dens bund, hvor den hang uden for skibssiden, og gned fedtet ind, som om han flittigt forsøgte at få en hårvækst til at gro på fartøjets skaldede køl. Han virkede, som om han handlede efter en bestemt forudanelse. Og det, der fulgte, viste heller ikke, at den var ubegrundet.
Henimod middag blev der set hvaler; men så snart skibet sejlede ned på dem, vendte de om og flygtede i hovedkuls hast — en forvirret flugt, som Kleopatras pramme ved Actium.

Alligevel tog bådene jagten op, og Stubbs båd var forrest. Med stor anstrengelse fik Tashtego til sidst sat ét jern; men den sårede hval, uden at dykke overhovedet, holdt sin vandrette flugt oppe, endnu hurtigere end før. Så uafbrudt et træk i det fastsatte jern må før eller siden uundgåeligt rive det løs. Det blev nødvendigt at lansere den flygtende hval eller finde sig i at miste den. Men det var umuligt at hale båden op til hans side; han svømmede så hurtigt og rasende. Hvad var der så tilbage?

Af alle de vidunderlige kunstgreb og færdigheder, de fingernemme tricks og utallige finesser, som den erfarne hvalfanger så ofte er nødt til at tage til, overgår ingen det fine lansemanøvre, der kaldes pitchpoling. Hverken en lille kårde eller et bredsværd kan i alle deres øvelser prale af noget lignende. Det er kun uundværligt ved en hval, der er en stædig løber; dens store kendetegn og kendsgerning er den vidunderlige afstand, som den lange lanse kastes nøjagtigt over fra en voldsomt slingrende, rykkende båd, der suser fremad for fuld fart. Med stål og træ iberegnet er hele spyddet nogle ti eller tolv fod langt; skaftet er meget spinklere end harpunens og af et lettere materiale også — fyr. Det er forsynet med et lille reb af betydelig længde, kaldet en warp, hvormed det kan hales tilbage til hånden efter kastet.

Men før vi går videre, er det vigtigt her at nævne, at selv om harpunen kan pitchpoles på samme måde som lansen, sker det sjældent; og når det sker, lykkes det endnu sjældnere, på grund af harpunens større vægt og kortere længde i forhold til lansen, hvilket i praksis bliver alvorlige ulemper. Som en almindelig regel må man derfor først være fast i en hval, før nogen pitchpoling kommer på tale.

Se nu på Stubb — en mand, hvis humoristiske, rolige kulde og fatning i de værste nødsituationer gjorde ham særlig egnet til at udmærke sig ved pitchpoling. Se på ham: Han står oprejst i den slingrende stævn på den flyvende båd; indhyllet i fnuglet skum er den slæbende hval fyrre fod forude. Han håndterer den lange lanse let, kaster to eller tre gange et blik langs dens længde for at se, at den er helt lige, og Stubb fløjter og samler rullen af warpen op i den ene hånd, så han holder fast i dens frie ende og lader resten være uhindret. Så holder han lansen vinkelret foran midten af sin linning og sigter med den mod hvalen; og mens han holder den rettet mod ham, trykker han støt skaftenden ned i sin hånd og hæver dermed spidsen, indtil våbnet står pænt afbalanceret på hans håndflade, femten fod oppe i luften. Han minder dig lidt om en jonglør, der balancerer en lang stav på sin hage. I næste øjeblik, med en hurtig, navnløs impuls, spænder det blanke stål over den skummende afstand i en storslået, høj bue og dirrer i hvalens livsplet. I stedet for funklende vand sprøjter han nu rødt blod.

»Så røg hanen ud af ham!« råbte Stubb. »Det er den udødelige fjerde juli; alle fontæner må løbe med vin i dag! Bare det var gammel Orleans-whisky eller gammel Ohio eller uudsigelig gammel Monongahela! Så skulle du holde et krus op under strålen, Tashtego, knægt, og vi ville drikke en omgang af den! Ja, sandelig, mine drenge, vi ville brygge fin punch i den brede åbning af hans blæsehul der og af den levende punchebolle drikke det levende stof ned.«

Igen og igen, under den slags munter snak, gentages det behændige kast, og spyddet vender tilbage til sin herre som en mynde i en dygtig line. Den pinte hval går ind i sit raseri, sin dødskrampe; slæbelinen slækkes, og lanseføreren lader sig drive agterud, folder hænderne og ser tavst på, at uhyret dør.
